A genuinely severable secular claim remains outside only if independently pleaded and resolvable without doctrine, ministerial fitness or leadership-selection adjudication; none is found here.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The jurisdictional characterization is vacated and merits dismissal of the selection-dependent Title VII claims is required. Eight Justices vacate the jurisdictional judgment and remand for substantive dismissal; Stone-Zsela would additionally affirm the dismissal on the corrected merits basis. The controlling mandate orders no discrimination trial, reinstatement, compelled reconsideration or financial relief.

### Public-employee honoraria restrictions

#### United States v. National Treasury Employees Union

**Docket or dockets:** No. 93-1170.
**Decided:** February 22, 1995.

For the other questions in this decision, see Federal Courts — Scope of public-employee speech relief (The existing ban is unenforceable throughout the certified class; The injunction does not adjudicate the claims of unrepresented senior employees; Crane retains his individual relief without a grade-only remand).

##### A broad prospective honoraria ban requires justification for its actual speech burden

**Holding:** When the Government broadly restricts future compensated expression by its employees acting as citizens, Pickering requires a justification commensurate with the restriction's actual reach and burden on employees and listeners. Section 501(b)'s honoraria ban is unconstitutional as applied to the represented lower-level employees' protected expression unrelated to their employment because the record does not adequately connect that burden to actual or apparent misuse of office; narrower valid ethics restrictions remain available.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stevens's Part I, joined by Stone-Zsela, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer: six Justices.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Pickering v. Board of Education, 391 U.S. 563, supplies the employment balance, applied to the breadth of a prospective restriction. Connick v. Myers, 461 U.S. 138, supplies public-concern principles without limiting protected subjects to politics or workplace criticism. Waters v. Churchill, May 31, 1994, retains its distinct particular-speech and reasonable-account rules. Simon & Schuster v. Members of the New York State Crime Victims Board, December 10, 1991, supplies the relevance of financial burdens. Turner Broadcasting System v. FCC, June 27, 1994, preserves substantial but reviewable legislative predictive judgments; it does not decide this employment case.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Section 501(b) prohibits receipt of an honorarium by a Member, officer or employee; §505(2) excludes special Government employees as defined in 18 U.S.C. §202. Section 505(3) covers money or anything of value for an appearance, speech or article; a series falls within the definition if its subject directly relates to official duties or payment is because of governmental status. That parenthesis does not already restrict every single honorarium. Actual and necessary travel expenses for the individual and one relative are excluded to the extent another person pays or reimburses them, and otherwise deducted to the extent they are not paid or reimbursed. Travel expenses mean transportation, lodging and meals away from residence or principal employment.

Section 501(c) treats a payment on the individual's behalf to a §170(c) charitable organization as not received, subject to a $2,000 ceiling on each payment and no financial benefit to the individual, parent, sibling, spouse, child or dependent relative. Section 504(a) permits an Attorney General civil action and a civil penalty up to the greater of $10,000 or compensation received. Under §504(b), a written opinion from an entity identified by §503 protects its recipient and another covered person whose facts are materially indistinguishable from subsection (a)'s sanction only for conduct after issuance, in good faith and in accordance with the opinion's provisions and findings. These are qualified provisions, not general exemptions. The separate §501(a) high-level outside-income ceiling is not adjudicated.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The judgment is affirmed in part, reversed in part and remanded. Nonenforcement of the existing ban throughout the certified below-GS–16 class is preserved by five votes; Crane retains individual relief by six; relief for unrepresented senior employees is removed. Congressional and judicial coverage, §501(a)'s outside-income ceiling and valid independent ethics restrictions are not invalidated. No penalty or compensation award is entered.

### Religious exercise and statutory protection

#### Church of Scientology Flag Service Organization, Inc. v. City of Clearwater

**Docket or dockets:** No. 93-1062.
**Decided:** December 5, 1994.

##### RFRA governs future enforcement and requires application-specific adjudication

**Holding:** RFRA applies to the threatened future implementation of Clearwater's preexisting ordinance: the Church must establish a substantial burden on its religious exercise, after which Clearwater must produce evidence and persuade that applying that burden to this person furthers a compelling governmental interest by the least restrictive means. The adverse prospective determinations concerning the identifying disclosures designated as section 100.03(1)(a), (b), (c), and (j), and the written-refund-policy requirement in section 100.05(1)(g), must therefore be vacated for that inquiry, with ordinary Article III standing and appropriate-relief limits preserved.

**Proposition-level authority:** Opinion of the Court (O'Connor), eight Justices; Stone-Zsela does not join.

**Current-force modification:** City of Boerne v. Flores, decided June 25, 1997, prevents this prospective statutory application from governing future State or local RFRA claims resting only on Congress's Fourteenth Amendment §5 power. The completed judgment remains final; independent grounds and the statutory reasoning retain force within a valid field of operation. Boerne neither reopens the judgment nor decides federal RFRA or separate preserved claims.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- Landgraf v. USI Film Products, 511 U.S. 244 (1994): applies the distinction between future enforcement and new legal consequences for completed conduct, consistently with RFRA's express temporal direction; neither Landgraf's general framework nor its distinct relevant-activity rationale is enlarged.
- Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah, 508 U.S. 520 (1993): preserves its objective religious-targeting, substantial secular-underinclusion, and strict-scrutiny holdings; the statutory remand neither supplies a purpose finding nor converts the enactment-history discussion into a controlling test.
- Board of Education of Kiryas Joel Village School District v. Grumet, 512 U.S. 687 (1994): preserves the distinct denominational-allocation and unequal particular-grant rules; accommodation does not cure an establishment violation, and RFRA does not decide that constitutional question.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No final substantial-burden or justification finding is made for the surviving identifying or written-policy requirements. The Court does not decide RFRA's constitutionality, retrospective monetary liability, a general exemption from civil fraud law, the disputed sectarian purpose, the precise Florida severability boundary, the unreviewed general anti-fraud clause, or unpreserved hardship-discretion and procedural objections. Section 7 leaves the Establishment Clause unaffected; section 6(c) supplies no authority to burden religious belief.

Section 100.05(1)(g) requires written refund terms and conditions when a refund representation is made, but does not prohibit a statement made in good faith at that time. It prescribes no substantive refund policy and does not incorporate §100.05(1)(f)'s separate written-request and willful sixty-day nonpayment conditions. No promise to offer refunds is required.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The adverse prospective identifying-disclosure and written-refund-policy determinations are vacated for RFRA adjudication. Existing relief favorable to the Church and the purpose/severability remand remain undisturbed, without adoption of the lower constitutional rationales or renewed enforcement of provisions set aside below. The written-policy inquiry retains the contemporaneous good-faith proviso.

**Later-authority backlinks:** City of Boerne v. Flores, June 25, 1997, resolves the reserved §5 power question and limits future State and local applications at that scope.

#### Swanner v. Anchorage Equal Rights Commission

**Docket or dockets:** No. 94-124.
**Decided:** March 27, 1995.

##### RFRA requires a distinct inquiry into this application of the housing laws

**Holding:** For prospective enforcement of the marital-status housing prohibitions against Swanner, Swanner must establish a substantial burden on his religious exercise; if he does, the government must produce evidence and persuade that applying the burden to him furthers a compelling governmental interest by the least restrictive means. The adverse federal prospective-enforcement determination is vacated for that inquiry because commercial participation and a general prohibition of discrimination do not by themselves complete it; no exemption or ultimate statutory justification is decided.

**Proposition-level authority:** Opinion of the Court (O'Connor), joined by Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Thomas: five Justices.

**Current-force modification:** City of Boerne v. Flores, decided June 25, 1997, prevents this prospective statutory application from governing future State or local RFRA claims resting only on Congress's Fourteenth Amendment §5 power. The completed judgment remains final; independent grounds and the statutory reasoning retain force within a valid field of operation. The reserved federal constitutional claim and the distinct state-law and due-process grounds are not extinguished; no retrospective reopening or recovery is ordered.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- Church of Scientology Flag Service Organization, Inc. v. City of Clearwater, December 5, 1994: applies its prospective, claimant-specific RFRA inquiry and distinct burdens to the present housing enforcement; its reservations concerning RFRA's constitutionality and retrospective monetary liability remain.
- United States v. Lee, 455 U.S. 252: preserves its recognition that exemptions can impose religious limitations on third parties; commercial activity is not treated as categorical forfeiture under RFRA.
- Roberts v. United States Jaycees, 468 U.S. 609: recognizes the weight of protected access and injury from exclusion; it does not automatically decide justification under every antidiscrimination law.
- Employment Division v. Smith, 494 U.S. 872: its constitutional neutral-law rule does not replace the enacted RFRA inquiry; its constitutional holding remains unchanged.
- Church of the Lukumi Babalu Aye, Inc. v. City of Hialeah, June 11, 1993: preserves objective neutrality, comparable secular harm, and strict-scrutiny rules without deciding the constitutional claim here.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No final substantial-burden or justification finding is made. The Anchorage ordinance's distinct individual-home exception applies when the renter would share common living areas with the owner, lessor, manager, agent, or other person; no finding places Swanner within it, and its legal comparability cannot be assumed either way. The Court neither invalidates the housing provisions nor ranks all marital-status protections. It does not decide religious teaching or advocacy, religious-mission housing, intimate owner-occupied arrangements, RFRA's constitutionality, or retrospective monetary liability. Alaska statutory construction, the state constitutional ruling, and separate notice/delegation due-process rulings are outside reconsideration. The federal constitutional exemption claim is reserved.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The adverse federal prospective-enforcement determination is vacated and remanded for RFRA's separate burden and justification inquiries. No final exemption or constitutional free-exercise ruling is made. Alaska statutory, state-constitutional and separate notice/delegation rulings are not reconsidered; no retrospective monetary or penalty relief is adjudicated.

**Later-authority backlinks:** City of Boerne v. Flores, June 25, 1997, resolves the reserved §5 power question and limits future State and local applications at that scope.

### Truthful alcohol-content labeling

#### Rubin v. Coors Brewing Co.

**Docket or dockets:** No. 93-1631.
**Decided:** April 19, 1995.

##### The challenged scheme does not materially advance its asserted health interest

**Holding:** The Government may not suppress truthful, nonmisleading numerical alcohol-content statements on lawful malt-beverage labels unless the restriction directly and materially advances a substantial interest. Preventing strength competition and its health harms is substantial, but the challenged scheme fails that requirement on this record; predictive judgment is permissible, while abstract concern and unexplained inconsistencies do not establish the necessary connection.

**Proposition-level authority:** Opinion of the Court (Kennedy), eight Justices; Stevens concurs in the judgment only.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp. v. Public Service Commission, 447 U.S. 557: applies its substantial-interest and direct-advancement requirements.
- Edenfield v. Fane, April 26, 1993: applies the requirement of responsive justification for the actual commercial-speech restriction.
- Cincinnati v. Discovery Network, March 24, 1993, and Lanphere & Urbaniak v. Colorado, April 18, 1995: apply the requirement that the selected speech restriction address the demonstrated harm, without an all-sources-at-once rule.
- United States v. Edge Broadcasting Co., June 25, 1993: distinguishes its supported state-based scheme; its holding creates no categorical vice-speech exemption.

**Independent alternative holding:** Independently of the failure of material advancement, the categorical suppression of accurate numerical beer-label information lacks a reasonable fit to the asserted strength-competition harm in light of its unexplained breadth and workable measures directed more closely at that harm. Reasonable fit requires proportionality, not the least restrictive imaginable means, and the Court prescribes no particular substitute regulation.

**Proposition-level authority for alternative holding:** Opinion of the Court (Kennedy), eight Justices; Stevens concurs in the judgment only.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- Board of Trustees v. Fox, 492 U.S. 469: applies reasonable proportional fit and preserves rejection of a least-restrictive-means requirement.
- Discovery Network and Lanphere: apply their distinct fit inquiry to the burden and supported alternatives here.
- Ibanez v. Florida Department of Business and Professional Regulation, June 13, 1994: applies the need for justification responsive to the actual truthful-information burden.

##### The asserted need to assist state policy supplies no alternative justification on this record

**Holding:** Assuming the Government’s state-assistance rationale is properly considered, its unsubstantiated assertion that federal suppression of accurate label information is needed to facilitate state alcohol policy does not justify this restriction. Legitimate accommodation of differing state policies remains possible when its need and operation are supported; federalism and the Twenty-first Amendment do not alone replace First Amendment scrutiny.

**Proposition-level authority:** Opinion of the Court (Kennedy), eight Justices; Stevens concurs in the judgment only.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- Edge Broadcasting: preserves the legitimacy of supported state-policy accommodation while distinguishing the missing demonstrated mechanism here.
- Central Hudson: requires the asserted justification to support the actual speech restriction rather than stand as an unexamined label.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The judgment sustaining the injunction against the challenged numerical label ban is affirmed, 9–0. The unappealed advertising judgment and separate state, descriptive-strength and design provisions remain undisturbed. No national format, alcohol ceiling, tax or replacement regulation is prescribed.

### Campaign financing, intermediary contributions and nonprofit advocacy

#### Day v. Holahan

**Docket or dockets:** No. 94-672.
**Decided:** May 15, 1995.

##### Authority of the responsive-financing judgment

**Authority of the judgment:** The section 10A.25(13) responsive-financing invalidation is affirmed 5–4: Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas support the judgment. Kennedy's plurality, joined by O'Connor, Scalia and Thomas, treats the adverse proportional legal trigger as an expressive burden; Stone-Zsela's judgment concurrence rests on insufficient programmatic connection on this record and rejects categorical invalidity. Neither framework controls, and no controlling rationale is established under Marks. The judgment binds the parties; the three independently majority-supported holdings below do not supply a unified financing rule.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The invalidated section 10A.25(13) mechanism increases candidate limits by independent expenditures opposing the candidate plus expenditures for the candidate's major-party opponents, excluding an association's communications solely to its dues-paying members. The provision itself has no $100 threshold; that figure describes the lower court's operational reporting scenario. The Board must notify every candidate in the race within 48 hours after receipt of the report or notice under section 10A.20(3), (6) or (6b), and within three days after notice must pay half the expenditure only to a subsidy-eligible candidate who has raised twice the minimum match, from an appropriation from the general fund. The lower court's electoral-result-eligibility concern describes implementation; it is neither a statutory payment exception nor a finding that every subsidy is immediately payable.

##### The special immediate-notice obligation falls with this trigger

**Holding:** Section 10A.20, subdivision 6b's additional immediate affidavit and service obligation cannot be enforced independently of the invalid responsive-financing mechanism on this scheme's demonstrated function and legislative relationship. Under Minnesota section 645.20, the special mechanism is essentially and inseparably connected with the invalid provision such that the legislature cannot be presumed to have enacted it alone; ordinary campaign reports remain enforceable within their separate terms.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stone-Zsela's Opinion of the Court, Part II, joined by O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas: five direct votes. Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer dissent on this component.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The additional obligation is a twenty-four-hour affidavit and service on the candidates and campaign treasurers in the affected race. The holding rests on essential legislative connection under section 645.20, not physical impossibility of reporting. The independent vagueness and overbreadth theories are not reached.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- Buckley, 424 U.S. 1: preserves distinct disclosure interests and associational protections; no categorical disclosure invalidation follows.
- Gibson, 372 U.S. 539: applies the need for a substantial relation between information demanded and the legitimate subject; does not eliminate ordinary reports.
- Brown v. Socialist Workers, 459 U.S. 87: recognizes genuine disclosure interests with protection for demonstrated associational harms; no new general exemption is created.

##### This $100 intermediary-contribution ceiling lacks sufficient fit

**Holding:** Minnesota's $100 annual ceiling on contributions received by the covered political committees and political funds is unconstitutional on the established burden and insufficiently fitted corruption/circumvention justification. Contributions remain distinct from independent expenditures: realistic routes around valid candidate limits may be regulated, but a broadly restrictive ceiling must preserve meaningful collective political association and fit an identified corruption or circumvention mechanism; no permanent dollar minimum follows.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stone-Zsela's Opinion of the Court, Part III, joined by Stevens, O'Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer: nine direct votes, at this stated functional application.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Section 10A.27(12) covers aggregate annual contributions from individuals, political committees and political funds, but excludes a candidate's principal campaign committee and a political party unit defined in section 10A.275 from its covered recipients. Higher limits, coordination controls, candidate transfers and demonstrated conduit restrictions remain open. The record's substantial pooling burden does not establish a permanent constitutional dollar floor or equate contributions with independent expenditures.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- Buckley: applies contribution/expenditure distinction, corruption fit and effective collective advocacy; its historical dollar figure is no minimum.
- California Medical, 453 U.S. 182: preserves candidate-transfer anticircumvention regulation; its plurality is not a categorical answer for every committee.
- Citizens Against Rent Control, 454 U.S. 290: applies protection of pooling for collective political expression; does not immunize a candidate-contribution conduit.
- NCPAC, 470 U.S. 480: preserves independent advocacy at its scope; contributions are not silently equated with expenditures.

##### MCCL receives protection on its actual nonprofit characteristics

**Holding:** Minnesota may not prohibit MCCL's independent expenditures solely because its incidental business activity and absence of a formal policy against significant corporate contributions fall outside section 211B.15, subdivision 15's literal safe harbor. On the undisputed minimal-business-income and insignificant-corporate-funding record, its relevant political-association characteristics support as-applied MCFL protection; material commercial accumulation, economic claimants or corporate/union conduit funding requires a different assessment.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stone-Zsela's Opinion of the Court, Part IV, joined by all eight Associates: nine direct votes on this as-applied holding. No general overruling or endorsement beyond Austin's surviving scope is adopted.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The section 211B.15(15) safe harbor requires no business activity, no economic shareholders or claimants, no establishment by a business corporation or union, and a policy against significant contributions from them. Protection rests on MCCL's actual minimal business income and undisputed insignificant corporate funding. That checklist cannot foreclose this as-applied protection; materially changed operations or corporate or union financing may require reassessment. Direct corporate candidate contributions and ordinary business-corporation treasury restrictions are not decided.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- MCFL, 479 U.S. 238: applies protection to actual political-resource, structure and funding characteristics; descriptive facts do not foreclose this narrow as-applied claim.
- Austin, 494 U.S. 652: distinguishes materially different commercially accumulated corporate wealth; its surviving corporate-treasury rule is not overruled.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Affirm the Eighth Circuit on all four components. Maintain the permanent restraints on section 10A.25(13)'s responsive financing, section 10A.20(6b)'s linked special notice and section 10A.27(12)'s $100 annual ceiling, and MCCL's bounded as-applied protection under section 211B.15(15). Ordinary reports and otherwise lawful corporate and contribution regulation remain; no damages, general public-financing prohibition or facial excision of corporate restrictions follows.

### Official confidential access and obstructive speech

#### United States v. Aguilar

**Docket or dockets:** No. 94-270.
**Decided:** June 21, 1995.

For the other questions in United States v. Aguilar, decided June 21, 1995, No. 94-270. see Criminal Procedure — Obstruction of judicial proceedings (A known nexus to pending judicial work); Criminal Procedure — Interception notice and obstructive purpose (Disclosure of a known application and obstructive purpose).

##### The as-applied speech objection

**Holding:** The First Amendment does not invalidate §2232(c) as applied to this purposefully obstructive notice by a judicial officer who acquired sensitive interception information through judicial office. This constitutional conclusion supports enforcement of the enacted application, knowledge and purpose elements; it creates no independent confidentiality offense or source-of-knowledge element.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg’s constitutional portion, joined by Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Breyer; eight Justices support the rationale. Stone-Zsela agrees only with rejection of the objection.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Accepted confidential official access and the enacted obstructive-purpose requirements define the as-applied holding. Ordinary public reporting, unrelated criticism and speech lacking the actual-application or obstructive-purpose predicates are not decided. No source-of-knowledge instruction or independent confidentiality crime is added.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- Smith v. Daily Mail Publishing Co.: distinguishes ordinary public dissemination from accepted official confidential access.
- Seattle Times Co. v. Rhinehart; Snepp v. United States: apply the accepted-access/confidentiality distinction at this as-applied level; create no independent offense here.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Affirm reversal of section 1503 Count 8 for insufficient charged judicial nexus. Reject the automatic expiration ground for section 2232(c) Count 6 and remand for preserved knowledge-instruction, harmlessness and other unresolved claims. Reinstatement remains conditional on those determinations and ordinary sentencing; no present reinstatement or commanded retrial follows. Acquitted or dismissed counts and the Government's sentencing appeal are not adjudicated.

### Private expressive composition and compelled inclusion

#### Hurley v. Irish-American Gay, Lesbian and Bisexual Group of Boston

**Docket or dockets:** No. 94-749.
**Decided:** June 19, 1995.

##### Private parade composition and compelled inclusion

**Holding:** Applying a public-accommodations law to compel private parade organizers to include an identified contingent conveying a message they do not choose violates the First Amendment. A parade remains expression despite broad admissions, multiple themes and the absence of a single precise message; the rule does not exempt ordinary nonexpressive goods or services from nondiscrimination law.

**Proposition-level authority:** Souter’s Opinion of the Court, joined by all eight other Justices; nine Justices adopt the as-applied private-expression holding.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Public-street use under a neutral permit does not convert this private parade into a governmental forum. The dismissed and unappealed state-action/public-forum theory against the City is not revived. Independent review of intertwined expression characterizations retains credibility deference. Message misattribution in other settings remains open; no general antidiscrimination exemption or premise that ordinary customer identity is itself a message is adopted.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- West Virginia State Board of Education v. Barnette: applies protection against compelled expression.
- Miami Herald Publishing Co. v. Tornillo: applies editorial selection protection.
- Turner Broadcasting System, Inc. v. FCC: applies existing medium-specific editorial protection, without importing unrelated cable results.
- Roberts v. United States Jaycees; PruneYard Shopping Center v. Robins: distinguish access not materially altering the private expressive composition.
- Bose Corp. v. Consumers Union; Fiske v. Kansas: apply independent review of intertwined First Amendment characterizations while retaining credibility deference.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Reverse and remand with the injunction compelling GLIB's inclusion dissolved. The public-accommodations law remains enforceable where its application does not compel private expression; no fee amount, fine or sanction is decided.

### Private religious displays in public forums

#### Capitol Square Review and Advisory Board v. Pinette

**Docket or dockets:** No. 94-780.
**Decided:** June 29, 1995.

For the other questions in Capitol Square Review and Advisory Board v. Pinette, decided June 29, 1995, No. 94-780. see Federal Courts — Mootness and seasonal permits (The expired permit dispute remains reviewable).

##### Ohio’s categorical Establishment Clause defense cannot sustain this exclusion

**Holding:** Ohio may not exclude this genuinely private religious display from Capitol Square’s actual, generally available forum on the categorical ground that its religious message and proximity to the Statehouse necessarily establish religion. The judgment concerns the proposal presented, including its offered private-attribution safeguard; it neither finds the later sign adequate nor creates an unconditional right to every unattended display.

**Proposition-level authority:** Stone, Parts II–III, joined by O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Souter, Thomas and Breyer: seven votes for this bounded speech and access holding. Those seven do not adopt one comprehensive Establishment Clause test.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The offered readable clarification of private sponsorship had negotiable wording; it is distinct from the later actual sign and the injunction's terms. No finding establishes approved final wording or the sign's adequacy. Government-sponsored displays, actual religious favoritism and future rules remain open. Parts II–III have seven direct joins; Part IV's four-vote contextual explanation and the three-vote private-access rationale supply no controlling comprehensive test or Marks subset. No categorical forum immunity or universal disclaimer requirement is adopted.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- Widmar v. Vincent: applies protection of religious expression in a genuinely open forum, while preserving examination of an actual establishment defense.
- Lamb’s Chapel v. Center Moriches Union Free School District: applies its controlling protection against exclusion of a religious perspective from comparable private access; its contextual reasoning is not converted into categorical forum immunity.
- Lemon v. Kurtzman and County of Allegheny v. ACLU: not overruled; the Court does not replace existing establishment law with a comprehensive test in this case.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Affirm the Sixth Circuit at the original scope of the Count One merits judgment: the December 21–24, 1993 permit period remains expired. No new permit, extension, sign condition, removal order, damages or remand is entered. Unappealed rally, damages and other matters remain outside review.

**Current-force modification:** Effective June 23, 1997, Lemon remains the governing Establishment Clause test as modified in Agostini v. Felton, Holding I. Purpose, effects and entanglement inform a single inquiry with three routes: controlling specific prohibition or distinct doctrine, established permissible relationship, and residual attribution and function. Clear cases apply that test; its former independent prongs do not remain a separate or fallback method. Pinette's bounded private-expression and access holding remains; it supplies no universal forum immunity or automatic attribution from location.

**Later-authority backlinks:** Agostini v. Felton; Chancellor, Board of Education of the City of New York v. Felton, Nos. 96-552 and 96-553, June 23, 1997, Holdings I–II; First Amendment — Public instruction on religious-school premises.

#### Chabad-Lubavitch of Georgia v. Miller

**Docket or dockets:** No. 93-1047.
**Decided:** June 29, 1995.

For the other questions in Chabad-Lubavitch of Georgia v. Miller, decided June 29, 1995, No. 93-1047. see Federal Courts — Mootness and seasonal permits (The recurring access dispute remains live, and only the Rotunda claim is reviewed).

##### Georgia’s categorical defense cannot sustain summary judgment excluding the private religious display

**Holding:** A State that actually opens a designated forum to comparable private unattended expression may not exclude an otherwise eligible religious viewpoint merely by asserting that its Capitol location necessarily establishes religion. On this record that categorical defense does not justify judgment for Georgia; lawful access must be provided on the neutral terms governing comparable private expression, with the actual form of relief left for proceedings below.

**Proposition-level authority:** Souter, Part II, joined by Stone, O’Connor, Scalia, Kennedy, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer: eight votes for this bounded judgment and speech holding; Stevens dissents from its application.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The indoor designated forum actually admits comparable sizeable unattended exhibits for several days. The Court does not endorse all the en banc reasoning or guarantee an unconditional display, and comparable secular access cannot be retained while excluding the otherwise eligible religious viewpoint.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- Perry Education Association v. Perry Local Educators’ Association: applies the actual designated-forum status and preserves lawful neutral management and prospective forum changes.
- Widmar v. Vincent and Lamb’s Chapel v. Center Moriches Union Free School District: apply protection of comparable private religious expression and the prohibition on religious viewpoint exclusion.
- Capitol Square Review and Advisory Board v. Pinette: applies the bounded rejection of a categorical establishment defense, not a universal forum exemption.

##### Interior location does not itself make clearly private expression governmental religion

**Holding:** Neutral access does not establish religion merely because a genuine private-expression forum lies inside a state capitol, when the actual context makes clear that the religious expression remains private rather than governmental. Actual selection, financing, control, adoption, preferential treatment or obscured private sponsorship can change that conclusion; neither a forum label nor any unspecified sign automatically resolves attribution.

**Proposition-level authority:** Souter, Part III, joined by Stone, O’Connor, Ginsburg and Breyer: five votes for this contextual rule. The additional decree-specific inquiry proposed in Part IV has only O’Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; it is not a five-Justice mandate.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The identifying greeting names Chabad but does not expressly disclaim state sponsorship; an offered disclaimer is not a finding of an effective completed safeguard. The four-Justice additional decree-specific attribution inquiry is not part of the mandate. Neither a universal sign duty, preferential religious access nor a duty to keep the forum open is imposed.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- County of Allegheny v. ACLU: preserves contextual examination of apparent governmental affiliation, rather than title alone.
- Capitol Square Review and Advisory Board v. Pinette: preserves its shared access holding and distinct attribution rationales; no categorical immunity is drawn from its separate opinions.
- Lemon v. Kurtzman: remains in force; no comprehensive replacement establishment test is adopted.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Affirm the Eleventh Circuit reversal of State summary judgment on Count II for further proceedings and lawful relief on neutral terms. No Supreme Court permit, retrospective 1991 display, fixed sign, permanent seasonal entitlement, damages amount or compulsory forum closure is ordered. Count I remains undisturbed; lawful physical, safety, scheduling and identification rules and genuinely prospective viewpoint-neutral forum closure or redefinition remain possible.

**Current-force modification:** Effective June 23, 1997, Lemon remains the governing Establishment Clause test as modified in Agostini v. Felton, Holding I. Purpose, effects and entanglement inform a single inquiry with three routes: controlling specific prohibition or distinct doctrine, established permissible relationship, and residual attribution and function. Clear cases apply that test; its former independent prongs do not remain a separate or fallback method. Chabad's contextual-attribution and access holding remains; location alone does not establish governmental sponsorship.

**Later-authority backlinks:** Agostini v. Felton; Chancellor, Board of Education of the City of New York v. Felton, Nos. 96-552 and 96-553, June 23, 1997, Holdings I–II; First Amendment — Public instruction on religious-school premises.

### Private student publications and religious viewpoints

#### Rosenberger v. Rector and Visitors of the University of Virginia

**Docket or dockets:** No. 94-329.
**Decided:** June 29, 1995.

##### Religious viewpoint in the private publication program

**Holding:** The University may not exclude an otherwise eligible private student publication from its generally available printing benefit because its editorial viewpoint is religious. The rule applies to this privately edited, independently attributed publication program on its otherwise lawful eligibility, payment and administrative terms; it does not require funding every religious activity or every subject.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy’s Opinion of the Court, joined by Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Scalia and Thomas; five Justices adopt the program-specific viewpoint rule.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Recognition, facilities, distribution and money remain distinct; not every public expenditure creates a speech forum. The publication remains independently edited and attributed under required disclaimers and approved vendor-payment terms.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- Perry Education Association v. Perry Local Educators’ Association: preserves limited-forum definition while forbidding viewpoint discrimination.
- Lamb’s Chapel v. Center Moriches; Widmar v. Vincent: apply private religious-viewpoint equality without assuming that facility access decides every subsidy.
- Regan v. Taxation With Representation: distinguishes definition of a government financing program from discriminatory exclusion within this opened private-publication arrangement.

##### Permissible printing support on the actual program terms

**Holding:** Providing this neutral printing benefit to the otherwise eligible private religious publication does not itself violate the Establishment Clause. Its secular student-expression purpose, broad neutral availability, independent editorial attribution and controlled vendor payments matter together; neutrality alone is not a universal authorization of devotional financing or governmental sponsorship of worship.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy’s Opinion of the Court; Stone-Zsela, O’Connor, Scalia and Thomas join this concrete program conclusion. Lemon remains governing law; no new universal framework is adopted.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The actual purpose, effect and entanglement inquiry remains; neutral availability alone neither authorizes unrestricted devotional financing nor governmental worship. Compelled-fee challenges, unrestricted religious aid and particular awards are outside review.

The denial concerned religious activity, defined by the Guidelines as primarily promoting or manifesting belief in or about deity or ultimate reality, rather than an established finding of religious-organization ineligibility. The organization rule separately concerns devotion as organizational purpose. Political restrictions separately exclude principal-purpose lobbying and candidate electioneering while permitting incidental or insubstantial advocacy, nonpartisan study/research and ideological views; those permissions are not exceptions to the religious-activity rule. Permitted ability-to-perform membership limits likewise remain distinct. Abandoned free-exercise/state individual-rights claims and unchallenged equal-protection intent findings are not reopened.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- Lemon v. Kurtzman: retains the existing purpose, effect and entanglement inquiry; no universal replacement is adopted.
- Witters v. Washington Department of Services for the Blind; Mueller v. Allen: apply neutral-benefit and private-direction distinctions within the actual program, not neutrality alone.
- Board of Education of Kiryas Joel v. Grumet: distinguishes denominational governmental authority and retains religious-neutrality limits.
- Zobrest v. Catalina Foothills: preserves the actual antecedent-law remand; supplies no religious-aid merits holding here.
- Lee v. Weisman: preserves limits on governmental religious participation and coercion; this private printing benefit compels no student worship.
- Church of Scientology v. Clearwater: distinguishes RFRA burdens and exemptions from constitutional financing authority.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Reverse and remand for removal of the religious-viewpoint exclusion under otherwise lawful eligibility, payment and administrative terms. Examine any properly available independent Virginia funding defense consistently with the federal viewpoint holding, without declaring applicability, validity or revival of forfeited defenses. No full payment, damages, immunity, fee or compelled-fee refund is determined.

**Current-force modification:** Effective June 23, 1997, Lemon remains the governing Establishment Clause test as modified in Agostini v. Felton, Holding I. Purpose, effects and entanglement inform a single inquiry with three routes: controlling specific prohibition or distinct doctrine, established permissible relationship, and residual attribution and function. Clear cases apply that test; its former independent prongs do not remain a separate or fallback method. Rosenberger's actual controlled vendor-funded printing benefit remains permissible on its program terms. It concerns financing, not merely facility access; it neither decided Agostini's public-teaching case nor authorized every devotional expenditure.

**Later-authority backlinks:** Agostini v. Felton; Chancellor, Board of Education of the City of New York v. Felton, Nos. 96-552 and 96-553, June 23, 1997, Holdings I–II; First Amendment — Public instruction on religious-school premises.

### Clinic access, expression and religious exercise

#### American Life League v. Reno

**Docket or dockets:** Fourth Circuit No. 94-1869; no separate Supreme Court merits docket established; judgment below, 47 F.3d 642.
**Decided:** November 13, 1995.

##### Facial speech challenge to the defined reproductive-service access restrictions

**Holding:** FACE's challenged service-related force, threat, physical-obstruction and intentional-property-damage provisions regulate access-related conduct without selecting a protected message. When the conduct is expressive, the defined harm, intent and alternative service-purpose requirements satisfy intermediate scrutiny because they further substantial access and safety interests unrelated to suppression, burden no substantially greater speech than necessary and leave usable nonobstructive communication.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy's Part II, unanimous.

**Material application:** Section 248(a)(1) requires force, threat of force or physical obstruction; intentional injury, intimidation, interference or attempt; and conduct because a person obtains or provides reproductive services, or intended to intimidate that person, another person or a class from doing so. Section (a)(3)'s reviewed branch separately reaches intentional facility-property damage or destruction, or attempt, because the facility provides those services. Interference restricts movement; intimidation means reasonable apprehension of bodily harm to oneself or another; obstruction makes ingress or egress impassable or passage to or from the facility unreasonably difficult or hazardous. Services include medical, surgical, counseling and referral services concerning reproduction, pregnancy or termination, including carrying pregnancy to term.

**Limits and questions not reached:** These qualifications govern all FACE holdings in this entry: a minor's parent or legal guardian is subject to no §248 penalty or civil remedy, including private damages and private or governmental injunctions, for described activity directed exclusively at that minor; no FACE remedy survives for that excepted conduct. Other law is not preempted, but no equivalent state remedy, general parental immunity or constitutional veto is presumed. The inclusive facility definition covers reproductive-service establishments and their building or structure, adding neither grounds nor worship premises. Separate passage language creates no interior-only limit, property-line rule or outdoor immunity; the worship branches remain unchallenged. Section 248(d)(1) preserves protected expression including peaceful picketing and demonstrations; (d)(2) separately creates no new remedy for interference with protected speech or religion outside a facility regardless of viewpoint and limits no existing remedy. Nonexclusive remedies, no preemption of state/local remedies, and preservation of state/local reproductive-service regulation retain their distinct terms. No numerical buffer, invitation rule, compulsory silence, discriminatory-enforcement ruling or resolution of materially different mixed-motive applications follows.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Affirm dismissal of the facial speech challenge. The other constitutional and categorical damages dismissals also stand; only RFRA receives the separate remand below.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Mitchell permits relevant motive accompanying proscribable conduct without ending scrutiny of expressive obstruction. O'Brien and Ward supply intermediate review; Turner requires actual classification and fit, not benign purpose alone. Madsen's more demanding injunction rule and distances are not transplanted. Hurley's private-expression protection remains; no expressive composition is compelled here.

##### Substantial overbreadth of the defined access restrictions

**Holding:** FACE's intentional-act and service-purpose requirements, defined access or bodily-harm predicates and textually available protection for First Amendment expression do not reach substantial protected expression relative to the law's legitimate sweep on this facial challenge. Political offense, persuasion and abstract belief alone are not violations; protected expression cannot itself become punishable merely because it proves relevant motive.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy's Part III-A, unanimous.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Relevant statements retain ordinary safeguards. True threats remain distinct from political hyperbole; no universal threat mental-state rule or particular uncharged-statement liability is decided. Applications actually punishing protected advocacy remain challengeable.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** R.A.V.'s controlling substantial-overbreadth rule applies; its separate content-selection opinion remains noncontrolling. Mitchell preserves relevant motive evidence without punishment of abstract belief and distinguishes speculative evidentiary chilling.

##### Facial vagueness of the defined conduct

**Holding:** The movement, passage and reasonable-apprehension-of-bodily-harm definitions, together with intentional conduct and required service-related purpose, provide ascertainable boundaries sufficient to defeat the presented facial vagueness claim. Offense, disagreement, resentment or persuasion alone does not satisfy them.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy's Part III-B; all eight Associates join. Stone-Zsela agrees only in the disposition.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Particular enforcement and threatening-statement questions remain; no actual criminal liability is adjudicated.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Cameron supports intelligibility of physical-obstruction restrictions in context. R.A.V.'s vagueness reservation survives; overbreadth is not substituted for this inquiry.

##### Categorical First Amendment challenge to elected statutory damages

**Holding:** Outside the parent/legal-guardian exception for activity directed exclusively at the actor's own minor, an otherwise eligible claimant may elect §248(c)(1)(B)'s $5,000 per violation before final judgment in lieu of actual compensatory damages. The First Amendment does not categorically require violation-based statutory damages to equal proved actual loss.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy's Part IV-A; all eight Associates join. Stone-Zsela joins rejection of the categorical challenge without a general statutory-damages rationale.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The election is permissive and replaces actual compensatory damages, not every other remedy. For §248(a)(1), the private civil claimant must be involved in providing or seeking to provide, or obtaining or seeking to obtain, services in a reproductive-health facility. No amount-specific reasonableness, entitlement, violation count, particular award, punitive damages or criminal sentence is decided. No private elected damages or other FACE relief survives the own-minor exception.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Claiborne forbids damages for protected persuasion and others' unlawful acts without attribution; it does not categorically prohibit a legislatively selected substitute for actual compensatory loss from an attributable violation.

##### Personal attribution of civil liability

**Holding:** FACE liability requires the defendant's legally attributable violation. Shared belief, membership, independent advocacy or another person's unlawful act alone is insufficient; protected persuasion that reduces demand cannot itself be the unlawful injury supporting an award.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy's Part IV-B, unanimous.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The Court determines no particular organizational responsibility, conspiracy, actual concert or individual award. An injunction's actual-concert rule does not supply damages liability predicates.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Claiborne preserves responsibility for unlawful conduct and protection for association and persuasion. Madsen's responsible-party and actual-concert restrictions remain injunction rules, not a new damages cause.

##### Facial religious targeting and the own-minor exemption

**Holding:** The challenged text establishes neither religious targeting nor a substantial exemption for comparable secular blockades: its predicates concern service-related acts and access, not religious identity. The parent/guardian exclusion of all penalties and civil remedies for activity directed exclusively at that person's own minor does not itself establish secular outsiders' permission to obstruct others' access.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy's Part V-A; all eight Associates join. Stone-Zsela agrees only in the constitutional free-exercise disposition.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Labor and environmental viewpoints receive no general statutory exemption; conduct with a different object may fail the enacted predicates. The full exclusion, including preventive injunctions, is considered, not misdescribed as a lower-penalty rule. No universal family-status exception to comparability, discriminatory-enforcement approval or finding that a plaintiff qualifies in another encounter follows. Its separate RFRA significance remains below.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Lukumi's objective text, operation, exemption and comparable-secular-harm inquiry applies. Religious prominence among opponents proves no targeting by itself; secular purpose language cannot save actual discrimination. Its noncontrolling legislative-purpose discussion is not substituted for the governing rule.

##### Broader constitutional exemption for the pleaded physical obstruction

**Holding:** Under Smith's neutral-law rule as bounded by Lukumi, the asserted religious obligation to engage in the covered physical obstruction supplies no constitutional exemption on the pleaded frame after the presented targeting and comparable-secular-exemption challenges fail. This does not decide RFRA or every materially different application.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy's Part V-B, joined by Stevens, Scalia, Thomas, Ginsburg and Breyer; six direct votes. O'Connor and Souter reserve the broader question; Stone-Zsela contributes no rationale.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The exclusively-own-minor exception is not a general secular blockade entitlement. Constitutional protection from discriminatory enforcement survives; RFRA's constitutionality is not decided.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Smith remains the constitutional neutral-law rule with Lukumi's targeting and general-applicability limits; Clearwater and Swanner require a separate statutory inquiry.

##### Person-and-application adjudication under RFRA

**Holding:** The RFRA prospective-enforcement dismissal must be vacated. The district court must identify each live claimant and threatened application, determine a genuinely disputed substantial burden, and, if established, require the Government to produce evidence and persuade that applying the burden to that person furthers a compelling interest by the least restrictive means, considering concrete alternatives and legally comparable exceptions.

**Proposition-level authority:** O'Connor's RFRA opinion, joined by Scalia, Kennedy, Souter and Thomas; five direct votes. Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Ginsburg and Breyer dissent from this remand.

**Material application:** General access, safety and health interests and successful intermediate speech scrutiny do not complete RFRA's application-specific showing. Reliable medical access and bodily safety carry compelling weight, and an accommodation may fail because it preserves the access injury; nonetheless, the complete parent/own-minor exclusion, even of preventive FACE injunctions, defeats an assumption of universal enforcement and requires actual comparison. Neither comparability with outsider blockades nor an equivalent state remedy is presumed.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Religious burden is assumed for review of dismissal, not found; sincerity and doctrinal necessity are not adjudicated. Claimants bear substantial burden, then Government bears production and persuasion on justification; claimants have no universal duty to prove alternatives. No mandatory hearing whenever religion is asserted, entitlement to blockade or redirect patients, final exemption or invalidation follows. RFRA applies to later federal law absent express exclusion by reference to RFRA; FACE contains none. Article III standing, appropriate relief, belief protection and the Establishment Clause remain distinct.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Remand only the RFRA prospective-enforcement claim. It may fail on the actual pleadings and a sufficient showing or at the substantial-burden threshold. No interim injunction follows automatically, and no new hearing or deadline is prescribed. The constitutional and categorical damages dismissals remain affirmed, each 9–0 in judgment.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Clearwater and Swanner preserve the actual-person/application inquiry and burden sequence. Smith does not replace RFRA. Lee and Roberts retain the significance of direct injury without creating a categorical statutory exception.

The commerce and federalism holding is under Constitutional Structure, American Life League, November 13, 1995, Fourth Circuit No. 94-1869.

### Civic observances in public schools

#### Sherman v. Community Consolidated School District 21 of Wheeling Township, judgment below 980 F.2d 437

**Docket or dockets:** Seventh Circuit No. 91-1684; no separate Supreme Court docket supplied.

**Decided:** February 12, 1996.

##### This voluntary civic Pledge is distinct from an official worship program

**Holding:** A public elementary school may conduct the daily civic Pledge containing the brief acknowledgment “under God” on this record, where the exercise expresses allegiance to the flag and Republic rather than conducting prayer, devotional instruction or a required religious profession, and pupils may decline words and gestures without punishment or forced exit. This permission does not authorize school-directed worship or compulsory assent merely because it appears within a patriotic program.

**Proposition-level authority:** O'Connor's Part I, joined by all seven other Associate Justices; eight Justices.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Government speech is at issue. The religious reference need not become meaningless to believers. Protected abstention matters within this civic exercise but does not cure actual school worship.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Engel and Schempp's official-prayer and devotional prohibitions, and Lee's official-sponsorship and independent religious-pressure holdings, remain intact. Lynch and Allegheny inform contextual civic acknowledgment; Good News and Pinette's private-expression rules do not characterize this government-selected exercise as private.

##### The program satisfies the existing contextual establishment inquiry

**Holding:** The challenged Pledge program serves a civic educational and ceremonial purpose, has no primary effect of governmental religious advancement in its actual use, and creates no religious-institutional entanglement. Its validity rests on that actual civic function and context, not on a universal historical exemption or voluntariness alone.

**Proposition-level authority:** O'Connor's Part II, joined by Stevens, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; five Justices. Kennedy, Scalia and Thomas withhold this comprehensive methodology while joining the concrete civic ground.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Possible disagreement or exclusion alone does not establish primary religious advancement; absence of supported hazing proof does not establish that every child feels no pressure. The decision reaches no universal historical exemption, other public motto, adult legislative prayer, historical-instruction or teacher-employment question.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Lemon's purpose, effect and entanglement inquiry is applied, informed by Lynch. Lee remains intact.

**Current-force modification:** Effective June 23, 1997, Lemon remains the governing Establishment Clause test as modified in Agostini v. Felton, Holding I. Purpose, effects and entanglement inform a single inquiry with three routes: controlling specific prohibition or distinct doctrine, established permissible relationship, and residual attribution and function. Clear cases apply that test; its former independent prongs do not remain a separate or fallback method.

**Later-authority backlinks:** Agostini v. Felton; Chancellor, Board of Education of the City of New York v. Felton, Nos. 96-552 and 96-553, June 23, 1997, Holdings I–II; First Amendment — Public instruction on religious-school premises.

##### Permission to conduct the program does not permit compelled affirmation

**Holding:** School officials may not require a pupil to recite the Pledge or make gestures affirming it, punish refusal, or require the pupil to leave as the price of declining participation. Because the established practice permits silence, remaining seated, declining the gesture and remaining in the room without penalty, the record supplies no compelled-affirmation ground for relief.

**Proposition-level authority:** O'Connor's Part I, joined by all seven other Associate Justices; eight direct opinion joins. Stone-Zsela independently accepts the compelled-personal-recitation conclusion but does not join the establishment rationale.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Barnette's protection against compelled words and gestures is applied and preserved.

**Operative remedy or transition:** School-program judgment affirmed, 8–1; no injunction or damages. The separate Attorney General dismissal remains undisturbed, unanimously, without a new holding on its grounds; the unappealed Society claim remains outside review.

### Indecent broadcasting and adult access

#### Action for Children's Television v. FCC; Pacifica Foundation v. FCC, judgment below 58 F.3d 654

**Docket or dockets:** D.C. Circuit Nos. 93-1092 and 93-1100; no separate Supreme Court docket assigned.

**Decided:** March 4, 1996.

##### The controlling review of protected nonobscene indecent broadcasting

**Holding:** Nonobscene indecent expression is protected. Content-selected restrictions must be carefully tailored to a compelling interest, with independent review of necessity and means in light of broadcasting's actual characteristics. Protecting children and assisting parental supervision are compelling interests but do not themselves establish this schedule's necessity.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's Part I, joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Kennedy, Souter and Thomas; six Justices.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Predictive legislative judgments receive substantial consideration but not conclusive effect. Scientific certainty and a particular legislative report are not indispensable; material differences between broadcast and telephone services remain.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Pacifica's contextual holding supplies no general timetable approval. Sable protects adult access and careful tailoring; Turner preserves deferential but independent review without transferring its content-neutral cable intermediate test or four-Justice insufficiency application.

##### Whether the mandatory 6 a.m.–10 p.m. schedule is sufficiently tailored

**Holding:** The mandatory sixteen-hour exclusion insufficiently fits the record justification for its broad burden on protected adult broadcasting and is unconstitutional. Substantial child access, late audiences and supervisory difficulties do not establish the necessary connection to this general exclusion across media and contexts.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's Part II, joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Kennedy and Thomas; five Justices. Souter's separate renewed-review vacatur is not a sixth vote for invalidity.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The contextual definition and attention to reasonable licensee judgment, clinical and bona fide news applications create no blanket news or serious-merit exception. The tentative defense allows market-wide proof of no appreciable child audience; ordinary station/program ratings remain inadequate absent convincing proof of relevance despite grazing. No automatic low-ratings exemption or individual defense is established. The decision requires neither proof of harm from every program nor flawless alternatives and does not make all media interchangeable. Facial vagueness and particular sanctions remain undecided.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** Butler protects adults against confinement to children's material without prescribing hours. Pacifica and Red Lion are not overruled; Pacifica's three-Justice speech-value discussion is not made controlling.

##### The mandatory remedy and continuing nighttime protection

**Holding:** The appellate approval must be set aside, the corresponding FCC rule removed and §16(a)'s dependent command barred insofar as it requires the invalid 6 a.m.–10 p.m. schedule. The existing uniform 10 p.m.–6 a.m. protection and rejection of the favored-station distinction remain undisturbed.

**Proposition-level authority:** Ginsburg's Part III, joined by Stone-Zsela, O'Connor, Kennedy and Thomas, supplies five direct votes for final invalidity and mandatory removal; all nine preserve nighttime protection. Stone-Zsela calls the action on appellate approval vacatur and the other four reversal; their operative removal direction is identical. Souter does not join it.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The original §16(a) distinction covered public stations signing off at or before midnight from 6 a.m.–10 p.m., and other stations from 6 a.m.–midnight. The Government did not cross-petition to restore the harsher decree. Section 16(b)'s repeal of the all-day restriction remains. Section 551's conditional parental-choice provisions establish no presently effective technological alternative, repeal, mootness or automatic remand; no device-system factual premise is adopted. No replacement hour, station permission hearing, general new definition or automatic serious-merit defense is prescribed.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Remand through the D.C. Circuit for mandatory set-aside relief. Independently lawful FCC authority, §1464 and ordinary obscenity enforcement remain, but the invalid restriction cannot be reproduced under another label. No individual sanction, damages or later technology implementation is decided.

**Treatment of earlier authority:** X-Citement Video permits alternative defense of an existing judgment but not enlargement without the necessary petition. Chesapeake's actual-repeal remand does not follow from §551 alone. No Marks aggregation makes Souter's distinct validity-open remand controlling.

### Cable access and protected indecency

#### Denver Area Educational Telecommunications Consortium, Inc. v. FCC; Alliance for Community Media v. FCC, 518 U.S. 727 (1996)

**Docket or dockets:** Nos. 95-124 and 95-227.
**Decided:** June 28, 1996.

##### Whether 1992 §10(a)’s leased-access permission is facially invalid

**Authority of the judgment:** The facial challenge fails, 6–3: Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Souter, Thomas and Breyer sustain §10(a); Stone-Zsela, Kennedy and Ginsburg would invalidate it. No controlling sufficient rationale exists under Marks. Souter’s contextual accommodation rationale has Stevens, O’Connor and Breyer; Scalia and Thomas instead rely on the absence of a freestanding right to compel an unwilling private editor. Neither rationale is established as a logical subset of the other. The component judgment does not establish a general permission-review framework.

**Limits and questions not reached:** The retained permission allows, but does not require, prospective enforcement of a written and published policy prohibiting programming reasonably believed to depict or describe sexual/excretory activities or organs in a patently offensive manner under contemporary community standards, specified by the FCC for cable. Protected nonobscene indecency is included; this is not Miller’s full obscenity test and has no categorical serious literary, artistic, political or scientific value exemption, although context matters. No universal validation of indecency definitions, certification, actual policies or genuinely governmental facilities follows.

##### Whether §10(b)’s compulsory identification, segregation and opt-in arrangement violates the First Amendment

**Holding:** When covered leased-access programming is not voluntarily prohibited under §10(a), the government may not impose this integral identification/notification, channel-segregation, default-blocking and advance written-election system. Its cumulative burden on willing speakers and adult recipients fails independent necessity and means review despite compelling child-protection and parental-assistance interests.

**Proposition-level authority:** Souter’s Part III and V-B, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O’Connor, Kennedy, Ginsburg and Breyer; seven Justices.

**Material application:** Programmers identify and notify; operators concentrate covered speech on blocked capacity. Access requires a written request and FCC-required statement of adult age, fulfilled within thirty days, not a mandatory thirty-day wait; another blocked channel may be used if capacity is insufficient. The operator-installed lockbox accommodation described for systems without premium/pay-per-view channels leaves the operator holding the key/code pending a request and retains default denial and written opt-in. It differs from a household-controlled device. Mixed unpredictable programming creates real parental difficulty but does not justify the integral design’s delay, deterrence and channel-wide burdens. Household controls remain usable after opt-in.

**Limits and questions not reached:** No finding supplies a public registry, universal affordability, perfect technical alternative, implementation of 1996 blocking laws or absence of all supporting evidence. Ordinary age checks, notices, voluntary requests, subscription mechanisms and blocking devices are not individually held unconstitutional. No additional vagueness, prior-restraint or certification ruling is necessary.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Approval reversed, 7–2; the integral compulsory scheme and corresponding rules must be set aside, without a judicial replacement design.

##### Whether §10(c) may authorize suppression of protected indecency on PEG access capacity

**Authority of the judgment:** Approval is reversed within the protected nonobscene-indecency scope, 6–3: Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Kennedy, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer support relief; O’Connor, Scalia and Thomas oppose it. Souter/Stevens/Breyer’s contextual means/attribution ground and Kennedy/Stone-Zsela/Ginsburg’s strict legislative-content ground each have three votes. Neither is a demonstrated logical subset of the other; no controlling sufficient rationale exists under Marks, and no universal PEG public-forum or state-action rule is adopted.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Section 10(c) directs enabling rules concerning obscenity, sexually explicit conduct and unlawful-conduct solicitation/promotion; it does not compel operator censorship. The FCC interprets sexual explicitness through indecency and the unlawful-conduct category as otherwise proscribed material, permitting operator content certifications. Section (c) lacks (a)’s written/published-policy and reasonable-belief limits and (b)’s subscriber machinery. Lawful obscenity controls remain; unlawful solicitation and freestanding certification are not independently adjudicated, and protected advocacy is not automatically unlawful solicitation.

**Operative remedy or transition:** The corresponding rule must be set aside to the extent it authorizes protected-indecency suppression. This is final relief implementing the component judgment, not a remand to reconsider constitutionality after a universal franchise inquiry.

##### Whether §10(a) remains operative and what the judgment reaches

**Holding:** Section 10(a) remains independently operative after §10(b)’s removal. The permission’s independent operation and Congress’s purposes permit severance; the invalid compulsory scheme is removed as an integral whole.

**Proposition-level authority:** Souter’s V-A, joined by Stevens, O’Connor, Scalia, Thomas and Breyer; six Justices. The seven-Justice V-B coalition controls removal of (b). All nine accept V-D’s boundaries of the adjudicated issues without opponents thereby joining invalidity of a disputed component.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Section 10(d)’s obscenity exception to access-programming immunity remains and is not general liability for protected indecency. Independent 1996 §506(a) permits refusal on public-access capacity for obscenity, indecency or nudity; its public-access language does not automatically cover all educational/governmental capacity. Section 506(b) separately covers leased access. Neither commands refusal nor imports the 1992 policy/request conditions; their constitutionality and application are not decided or extinguished. Sections 504 and 505 retain their distinct subscriber-request/no-charge and sexually-oriented-channel triggers and transitions; their enactment proves no technical efficacy or actual implementation. Act §561’s three-judge facial-review route is not a new proceeding here. No unconditional carriage right, general private-editor immunity, universal forum designation, damages, new FCC hearing or automatic interim relief follows.

**Operative remedy or transition:** Remand to implement the three distinct component results within the challenged 1992 authorities.

**Treatment of earlier authority:**

- **ACT/Pacifica (March 4, 1996):** The Court applies its protection of nonobscene indecency and independent necessity/means review to the compulsory (b) arrangement. Its broadcast timetable disposition is not a cable rule. The divided permission opinions preserve the governing protection while disagreeing on application.
- **FCC v. Pacifica Foundation:** Its narrow, contextual broadcast holding remains; it does not automatically sustain every cable indecency restriction or establish that the present protected speech is of lower constitutional value.
- **Sable Communications v. FCC:** The (b) majority applies the distinction between compelling protection of children and adequately justified restrictions on adults. Scalia's separate willing-outlet analysis concerns the permissions and is not the Court's sufficient (b) ground.
- **Turner Broadcasting:** Cable editorial interests retain ordinary speech protection. The prior content-neutral full-power must-carry classification and intermediate standard do not govern an expressly content-selected indecency scheme. Neither the earlier limited shared predictive-review principle nor its fractured record-insufficiency discussion requires remand in every cable case.
- **Hurley:** The protection of an actual private expressive presentation remains intact. The component opinions disagree about the legal consequences of access duties; none establishes that ownership alone makes every independent access program the operator's message.
- **Perry and Cornelius:** Their attention to the actual forum and government's arrangement remains. The Court creates no universal cable-access forum; Kennedy's conditional forum ground does not become such a holding.
- **Rosenberger, Pinette and Chabad:** Their program-specific viewpoint, attribution and contextual rules are not converted into a presumption that every regulated channel is a public forum or governmental speaker. The divided opinions' use of those limits creates no new general forum or attribution test.
- **Blum, Jackson and Lugar; Reitman and Crawford:** The distinction between a private act and governmental alteration or encouragement remains relevant. No categorical operator immunity or rule making every private refusal government action is adopted.
- **Alaska Airlines:** The Court applies independent operation and congressional intent in retaining (a) after invalidating (b).

No earlier decision is overruled. The separate opinions' broader grounds do not independently alter controlling law.

### Commercial speech and alcohol-price advertising

#### 44 Liquormart, Inc. v. Rhode Island, 517 U.S. 484

**Docket or dockets:** No. 94-1140.
**Decided:** May 13, 1996.

##### Material advancement and reasonable fit of truthful-price restrictions

**Holding:** Even under ordinary *Central Hudson* review and treating temperance as substantial, Rhode Island has not demonstrated that these truthful-price restrictions directly and materially reduce consumption. The holding concerns this record and restriction, not every possible effect of advertising, prices, or demand; supported prediction remains permissible without a mandatory state-specific numerical study or experimental certainty.

**Proposition-level authority:** Kennedy's Part I, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, Souter and Ginsburg; five. Stevens affirmatively adopts this independently sufficient conditional application without accepting consumer ignorance as legitimate or ordinary scrutiny as the complete constitutional account.

**Material application:** The State's search-cost/price-dispersion mechanism and opposing experts' concessions of price responsiveness and theoretical plausibility are material but do not overcome the trial finding of no significant consumption effect. General-advertising studies with control problems, missing estimates connecting this restriction's projected price change to consumption, and possible market-share gains without aggregate consumption gains fail to establish material advancement. Constitutional sufficiency is independently assessed without turning appellate economic inference into a new trial finding.

**Independent alternative holding:** Even assuming material advancement, continuously suppressing this category of truthful retail-price information is disproportionate to the temperance objective on this record. Concrete direct price and tax alternatives expose inadequately justified fit; they are neither mandatory replacements nor a least-restrictive-means rule.

**Proposition-level authority for alternative holding:** Kennedy's Part II, joined by Stone-Zsela, Stevens, O'Connor, Souter, Ginsburg and Breyer; seven. O'Connor and Breyer assume advancement; Souter adopts both failures; Stevens's application remains conditional. Scalia's judgment vote and Thomas's categorical theory supply no additional balancing votes.

**Material application:** Interstate-shopping concerns do not explain why the State's indirect price mechanism avoids the same leakage or justify the informational burden. Section 3-8-7 permits merchandise-attached or merchandise-placed price signs or tags inside licensed premises under departmental rules; Regulation 32 forbids references visible from outside Class A premises. Section 3-8-8.1 separately excepts recognized, authorized trade journals. These exceptions and lawful nonprice promotion neither automatically defeat nor establish fit; the challenged category is complete subject to those exact exceptions, rather than a ban on all alcohol speech.

**Limits and questions not reached:** Ordinary *Central Hudson/Fox* review remains operative.
